cards.name: 6 pt
cards.summary: Sets the selected text (or, with no text selected, the size the next type you set starts at) to 6 pt, about 2.1 mm em height: the smallest preset, fine-print scale that most readers need to hold close.
use_for: legal disclaimers and copyright lines at the foot of an ad or packaging panel
ingredient or compliance text on a small label where space is the hard limit
registration marks, file slugs and printer notes outside the trim
avoid: reversed-out (white on dark) or thin/serif faces in print: 6 pt fills in and breaks up; go to 7-8 pt or a heavier weight
screen graphics (social posts, slides): 6 pt is unreadable at normal viewing size; use 14 pt or more
a selection holding several runs of different sizes: every run becomes the same size, so select only the run you mean to change

cards.name: Smart Punctuation...
cards.id: Adobe Illustrator Smart Punctuation Menu Item
cards.summary: Opens the Smart Punctuation dialog, which replaces typewriter characters with typographic ones in the selected text or the whole document: straight quotes to curly quotes, -- to en/em dashes, ... to an ellipsis, double spaces after a period to one, f-ligatures and expert fractions.
cards.how: Tick what to replace: ff/fi/ffi ligatures, ff/fl/ffl ligatures, Smart Quotes, Smart Spaces, En/Em Dashes, Ellipses, Expert Fractions. Replace In: Selected Text Only or Entire Document; Report Results lists the number of changes.
use_for: cleaning pasted copy from email or a plain-text brief before final layout
fixing straight quotes and apostrophes in headlines and pull quotes
a last typographic pass over a brochure or packaging copy before print
avoid: inch and foot marks or code samples that must keep straight quotes: run it on a selection, not the whole document
fonts without ligature or fraction glyphs: those replacements do nothing; prefer the OpenType panel options for fonts that have them

cards.name: Create
cards.summary: Threads (links) the selected text objects so one story flows from the first area or path type object into the next in stacking order; a plain closed path in the selection is turned into a new text area the overflow fills.
use_for: flowing a long article across columns or pages of a brochure or magazine spread
continuing overset copy from one text frame into a second shape
making text run from one frame on artboard 1 into a frame on artboard 2
avoid: point type in the selection: only area type and type on a path can thread; convert it with Type/Type Conversion first
an unexpected flow order: threads follow stacking order, so arrange the objects (or link by clicking the out port) before running it
a selection with no text object: there is nothing to flow

cards.name: Release Selection
cards.summary: Takes the selected object out of a text thread: its text reflows into the next object in the thread and the released object stays on the artboard as an empty text area.
use_for: dropping one column from a multi-column threaded layout without losing copy
removing a frame that was threaded by mistake
reusing a frame for different content while the story keeps flowing through the others
avoid: wanting every frame to keep the text it shows: use Type/Threaded Text/Remove Threading
releasing the last frame of a thread: its text goes back to overset in the previous frame; enlarge that frame first
a selection that is not part of a thread: nothing changes

cards.name: Remove Threading
cards.summary: Breaks every thread between the selected text objects while leaving the text where it currently sits, so each frame becomes an independent text object holding the lines it was showing.

splitting a threaded story into separate blocks to style or move them independently
preparing threaded text for export to formats or tools that do not keep threads
avoid: wanting to drop one frame and keep the rest flowing: use Type/Threaded Text/Release Selection
copy still being edited: once unthreaded, added text no longer flows to the next frame and overflows instead

cards.name: 3D Ribbon
cards.summary: Applies the 3D Ribbon effect to the selected type on a path: each character keeps its horizontal edges perfectly horizontal while its vertical edges lean perpendicular to the path, so the line looks like a twisting ribbon seen in perspective.
use_for: ribbon and banner lettering on badges, labels and retro emblems
text that should look like it is printed on a waving flag or tape
playful headline text along a wavy path
avoid: tight curves or circles: letters shear heavily and collide; use Rainbow (the default) on circles
small text: the shear hurts legibility; keep it for display sizes

cards.name: Gravity
cards.summary: Applies the Gravity effect to the selected type on a path: each character's baseline centre sits on the path while its vertical edges are aimed at the path's centre point, so letters fan out or converge as if pulled toward that centre and the run takes on a warped, perspective-like look.
use_for: perspective-style lettering on an arc, such as text that seems to wrap around a sphere or bowl
stylised title text on a shallow curve for posters or album art
exaggerated fan-out text on badges and stamps
avoid: paths whose centre point is close to the text: letters distort strongly; try Rainbow or Skew
body or small text: the distortion makes it hard to read

cards.name: Rainbow
cards.summary: Applies the Rainbow effect (Illustrator's default for type on a path) to the selected path type: each character's baseline lies parallel to the path at its position, so letters rotate smoothly with the curve.

avoid: sharp corners in the path: letters crowd or gap at the corner; add Spacing in Type on a Path Options or smooth the path
text that must stay upright (signage on stairs-like layouts): use Stair Step or Skew

cards.name: Skew
cards.summary: Applies the Skew effect to the selected type on a path: each character keeps its vertical edges perfectly vertical while its horizontal edges follow the path, so letters are sheared up and down with the curve instead of rotated.

text that follows a gentle wave or slope, like a flag or a sound-wave graphic
retro display lettering with a sheared, rising baseline
avoid: steep or vertical path sections: the shear becomes extreme and letters flatten; keep the path shallow
circular text: use Rainbow

cards.name: Stair Step

text that follows a rising or falling line in an infographic while keeping letters level

cards.name: Type on a Path Options...
cards.path: Type/Type on a Path/Type on a Path Options...
cards.summary: Opens the Type on a Path Options dialog for the selected path type, where its effect, flip, vertical alignment to the path and spacing around curves are set together with a live preview.
cards.how: Effect: Rainbow, Skew, 3D Ribbon, Stair Step or Gravity. Flip: moves the text to the other side of the path and reverses its direction. Align to Path: Ascender, Descender, Center or Baseline decides which part of the letters sits on the path. Spacing (pt): tightens letter spacing around sharp curves. Tick Preview to see changes before OK.
use_for: putting text on the inside bottom of a circular badge (Flip plus Align to Path: Ascender)
centring lettering on a stroked path so the stroke runs through the text middle (Align to Path: Center)
evening out letter spacing on tight curves of circular text
avoid: point or area type selected: the dialog only applies to type on a path; create it with the Type on a Path tool
using Spacing to loosen or tighten the whole line: it only changes the gaps around sharp curves and corners, not straight runs; set overall letter spacing with Tracking in the Character panel

cards.name: Horizontal
cards.summary: Sets the selected type object to horizontal orientation, so characters run left to right in lines stacked top to bottom; turns vertical type back into normal horizontal type.
use_for: reverting text that was set vertically by mistake

avoid: wanting the whole text block rotated 90 degrees: orientation changes reading direction, not the object's angle; rotate with Object/Transform/Rotate... instead

cards.name: Vertical
cards.summary: Sets the selected type object to vertical orientation, so characters stack top to bottom in columns that run right to left. Latin letters run down the column one under another; whether half-width (Roman) characters stand upright or turn sideways follows the Character panel's Standard Vertical Roman Alignment setting.
use_for: Japanese, Chinese or Korean vertical text in packaging and posters
stacked-letter signage and narrow vertical banners (shop fascia, spine of a book)
vertical labels on tall infographic bars
avoid: Latin text meant to read sideways along a spine: rotate horizontal type 90 degrees instead of stacking letters
long Latin passages: stacked letters read slowly; keep vertical setting to a few words or to CJK copy
